sources.rationale: getpass.getpass exists to read a password without echoing it — its return value is a credential by contract, the strongest secret source the stdlib has.

Environment variables are the dominant credential channel in deployed services. The format matches the call, not the key, so this seeds EVERY env read — heuristic-grade breadth the class tag carries so downstream consumers can weigh non-credential keys accordingly.
Module-level spelling of the same env read; the two spellings are interchangeable at call sites, so covering one without the other would make coverage depend on style.
keyring.get_password(service, username) returns the stored credential from the system keyring — a secret by API contract, exact-name matchable at module level.
Session.get_credentials returns the resolved AWS access key, secret key and token; anything derived from it is credential material.

sinks.rationale: Module-level logging writes to whatever handlers ship the log stream; a secret in the message or in the printf-style arguments (positions 1+ format into the message) persists wherever logs land. Class-gated: only secret-classed flows are this defect — logging other tracked values is not a CWE-532 exposure.
Debug-level logging is where credentials get printed deliberately during bring-up and then shipped; same message-plus-format-arguments surface as logging.info, same secret-class gate.

logging.exception logs the message AND the active traceback, so a secret in either the arguments or the raised exception's text lands in the log stream. Same secret-class gate as the other logging entries.

The getLogger instance idiom (logger.info) is the common real-world logging spelling and has no import binding to resolve; bare-name equality gated on a receiver named logger, hence heuristic. Secret-class gated like the module-level entries.
Instance spelling of the debug-level surface, same receiver-named-logger gate, heuristic confidence and secret-class gate as the info entry.

print writes to stdout, which in services is captured as logs; it is also the single most common call in Python, so the claim is deliberately heuristic-confidence and secret-class gated — a hit means a secret reached stdout, not that stdout is always a log.

A credential encoded into a query string travels in URLs — access logs, proxies, referer headers all record it. urlencode is the stdlib chokepoint where values become query text; the gate keeps the claim to credential-classed values.

An exception message surfaces in tracebacks, error pages and logging.exception output; building one from a secret puts the secret on all of them. Class-gated because only secret-classed flows are this defect — exception text routinely carries benign values.

Command-line arguments are visible to every local user via the process table. This claim is about argv VISIBILITY of a credential, so it is secret-class gated (a non-secret flow into the same callee is the command-injection entry's claim, not this one) and, unlike that entry, carries no shell=False suppression — a literal shell=False changes interpretation, not visibility.

sanitizers.rationale: scrubadub.clean(text) replaces the PII its detectors find — whether a given credential shape is among them depends on configured detectors, so the flow stays alive with the redaction hop recorded rather than killed.

Presidio anonymizes exactly the analyzer_results spans it is handed; redaction completeness is a call-site property, so the hop is recorded and the flow kept for downstream judgement rather than killed.
